subject: Single season occupancy model convergence, random effects issues

messages.author: 639259235f317e0d
messages.subject: Single season occupancy model convergence, random effects issues
parts:
Hello. 

I'm trying to build single season occupancy models for a few different datasets:

1) 30 streams/ditches, two surveys per period, 37 total periods (a few sites were surveyed in two periods for all of three of these datasets), 25 total detections at 20/30 sites, with mostly landcover based predictors 
2) 22 streams/ditches,  two surveys per period, 28 total periods, 20 total detections at 14/22 sites, with quantitative and qualitative habitat as well as landcover based predictors
3) 22 ponds/lentic wetlands, two surveys per period, 30 total periods,  28 total detections at 14/22 sites, with some microhabitat, qualitative habitat, and landcover based predictors, with quantitative and qualitative habitat as well as landcover based predictors

I centered and standardized all continuous covariates and checked covariates for co-linearity.

In each case, when I use Site as a random intercept effect, only a few univariate psi models converge and only one of those has a significant coefficient (although I have read that significance is approximate for mixed models?). In most cases, I get system is computationally singular, Hessian is singular, NaNs produced, or model did not converge errors.

When I omit random effects and only use one period per site, I can use more predictors (still not more than 2-4 in most cases) before getting the above errors, but I still get high p-values for almost all predictors and detection covariates especially. 

Are these errors expected with my low sample sizes/survey replication, potentially high occupancy? Or is it just likely that my predictors are uninformative? Also, I'm not sure whether I'm using random effects appropriately in this case. I couldn't find much information about using random effects in occupancy models.

Thank you,
Sean

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Single season occupancy model convergence, random effects issues
parts:
Dear Sean,

I have three comments:
  1. I think it would be good if you state, perhaps right in the header of the email, whether your question refers to unmarked or ubms. This helps to get into the right "state of mind".
  2. You have extremely sparse information about occurrence. Look at this: there is a sense in which a single-species occupancy model is a combination of two logistic regressions:
  • one is for the presence/absence of the species at a site, except that you only observe the site occupancy state in an imperfect manner, and have to estimate it
  • the other is for the actual detection/nondetection measurements, which are actual observed data
Your sample sizes for these two regressions are 22-30 for occupancy and between 500 and 1000 or so for detection. So, you have comparatively plenty of information to learn about the covariates that may affect detection, but you have extremely sparse data to learn about the factors associated with occupancy.

There are various rules of thumb about how many data points you need for each parameter in a regression model and I believe they range between 5 and 20 or so. So in your case, this would mean that you could add perhaps between 1 and 6 covariates into the occupancy model. BUT: you are in a worse position, since you haven't observed the presences and absences, but you must estimate them. So it is not so remarkable perhaps that you would get into problems when you try to estimate more than 1-2 or so covariates in the submodel for p.
  1. But perhaps the most important thing is that a static occupancy model with random site effects is not identifiable. I.e., you can't estimate these parameters. This is related to the usual GLM wisdom (which one can probably find somewhere in the McCullagh and Nelder bible or in some other GLM book) that you can't estimate overdispersion in a binary-response logistic regression.
Best regards  --- Marc

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Single season occupancy model convergence, random effects issues
parts:
Wanted to say: "....get into problems when you try to estimate more than 1-2 or so covariates in the submodel for PSI (and not p)."

Also, I just assumed that you put your site-level random effects in the occupancy part of the model, where this leads to non-identifiability. In contrast, site-level random effects in detection are perfectly fine, since the temporal replication of the typical occupancy data renders them identifiable.

Marc

messages.author: 4f80e1927b0757cb
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Single season occupancy model convergence, random effects issues
parts: I think it is theoretically possible to estimate a random site effect in this case, since in each dataset there were a handful of sites that were sampled during two different periods. However I agree with Marc that there simply isn't enough data available to get good estimates of a random site effect - you would need more sites and more periods per site. Hence the various non-convergence errors.

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Single season occupancy model convergence, random effects issues
parts:
Hi Marc and Ken.

Thank you very much for your thorough responses and the reference recommendation. I'll have to read more into binary-response logistic regression and overdispersion. I figured that I might have to downgrade from hierarchical occupancy estimation to biased estimation with a single logistic regression. Although I imagine my sample sizes are still small even for that. 

And Marc you are right that I was including the random effects in the occupancy part of the model.

My apologies for failing to state that I'm using unmarked for these occupancy models--I hadn't realized this group also addresses other packages.

Thank you again,
Sean
